title: I Let My Pi Agent DRIVE My Backtest Software.
author: Extreme_Leg_6162
selftext: Straight to the point, if you've ever rigourously defined and backtested a strategy, you know that there are multiple discrete and tedious steps that get you to the end result, and you also know that writing code for a "vague" strategy or a strategy that takes hours and hours of time to just represent precisely is a slow and boring job, as traders we optimize for speed and execution, not spending hours or days(or even weeks depending on the complexity of the strategy) trying to write a algorithm. My agent driver uses my specified backtester, and it will never ever run a backtest if I didn't review the code or code flow before execution, the agent essentially turns your plain langauge(english) into a strategy it can backtest, but before backtesting the agent asks if the code or code flow written is what you intended or whether you want to edit some parts using plain lanagauge.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
most agent backtest setups skip the review-before-run step, and it's where "buy the dip" turns into something you can actually argue with. I made the same choice building Quantradin: you describe the rule in normal English, it shows you the rule it understood, and it only replays history once you agree. free, quantradin.com.

when the agent misreads you, is it usually the entry or the exit?

replies.author: Extreme_Leg_6162
replies.body:
Whether it misreads a user(there is always a misread delta regardless of how small it can be, the machines are stochastic by design), depends entirely on how logical/precise your computer instructions were, I found that breaking down the strategy into a category and defining the transformation rules, usually something like S={signal space}, E={entry space},Ex={exit space}, then you precisely define f:S --> E as the entry function f(S) and g:E --> Ex as the exit function g(E), so the two functions compose like so g(f(S)) which is represented as g○f: S --> E --> Ex, is essentially a great framework for thinking about what the overall strategy space/entry/exit space is in terms of structure,  and the example functions domain/codomain are 1-dimensional but you can easily plug and play for n-dimensions where n > 1.  

Signal space is vast, entry space is vast, exit space is also vast, so being precise about what the signal is, what the entry is, and what the exit is the most important detail when it comes to letting agents drive.

comments.author: Zealou-sidealIron
comments.body: Love that it asks before running. Does it also show you the assumptions it picked on its own, like fees, slippage and fill prices? Those quiet defaults are usually what make a backtest look better than real life.

replies.author: Extreme_Leg_6162
replies.body:
The default parameters are the default parameters of the backtest software, so it doesn't make stuff up.

If you want to change them just be explicit about it in your computer instructions.

comments.author: QATSAlgo
comments.body: The review gate is useful. Could the approval attach to a specific code hash and data version, and become invalid after any edit? That would avoid approving one implementation and accidentally running another. A tiny hand-worked example with expected entry and exit timestamps would also help a non-programmer check what the agent understood. QATS team here; interested in the validation workflow.

replies.author: Extreme_Leg_6162
replies.body:
Interesting idea! I haven't added that feature, the Pi agent driver is still version 1.0. The tiny hand worked example is a interesting take, but without a precise mapping/function, what the agent "understood" is usually the low effort logic the average user usually gives it. But break down the intent into a precise and logical mathematical mapping with defined transformations and invariants and you essentially "shrink" the design space of the agent, and that's why "understanding" for a agent doesn't make sense in the technical sense, an agent will never understand something, they will only give you the highest probability output that matches what you asked for, which is why I always preach about breaking down intents into precise spaces that I can turn into mappings and functions with rigourous definitions, because if the agent can never "understand" something but only give out "high probability" outputs, the best way, at least to me, is to reduce how many outputs match my given intent, and only logic can do that. Vague lanaguage can't be fixed by a better model or a better software, a vague statement is a vague statement regardless of intent and that blows up the size of the output space to outputs that are most likely not what you want on average. 

It's a shift from high level programming languages(C,C++,python,etc...) to hyper programming(is what I call it), which is essentially replacing programming languages with pure logic, and by pure logic i mean pure logic, no hand waving, no undefined terms, no hope prompting, just a sharp and precise sequence of statements and structures that program the agent to "shrink" it's output space, the average user usually blows up the output space. 

I honestly think that's the future of programming, shrinking output space.
